# Pruning and Reduction

Also called: Gaussian Pruning, Scene Reduction, Visibility Filtering

## Overview
Pruning and reduction methods aim to decrease the storage footprint and computational cost of [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) representations by removing redundant or low-impact Gaussians, or by simplifying their attributes, without significantly degrading rendering quality. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on [opacity-based culling](#14501-opacity-culling.md) during rendering, these methods actively modify the scene representation during or after training. They are distinguished from sibling methods like [Inverse Multiquadric Splatting](9910-inverse-multiquadric-splatting.md) (which changes the kernel function) and [Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation](10266-opacity-independent-gaussian-truncation.md) (which changes the rendering integration bounds) by focusing on the selection or simplification of the Gaussian primitives themselves.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the standard [3D Gaussian Splatting representation](#2257-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs-preliminaries.md), where the scene is defined by a set of $N$ 3D Gaussians $\{G_i\}_{i=1}^N$ [S1, unofficial]. Each Gaussian $G_i$ is defined by its mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i$, covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ (derived from [rotation](#19376-rotation.md) $\mathbf{R}_i$ and scale $\mathbf{S}_i$), opacity $\alpha_i$, and view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ [S1, unofficial].

The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega$ and integrates contributions [G]. The Gaussian density function is:
$$ G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) $$

## Subtopics

### [Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting](13983-vertex-level-pruning-in-mixed-primitive-gaussian-splatting.md)
Vertex-level pruning is a refinement mechanism for Mixed-Primitive [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) (MP-GS) that removes redundant vertices from Gaussian triangles and lines during training to reduce storage overhead and simplify the scene representation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which only performs primitive-level [opacity pruning](#14627-opacity-pruning.md), this method dynamically converts primitives into lower-vertex forms (ellipses or lines) based on geometric proximity and collinearity. It complements [Attribute Pruning](18516-attribute-pruning.md) and [SplatQ](14415-splatq.md) by addressing topological redundancy in mixed primitives rather than [attribute quantization](#1912-attribute-quantization.md) or opacity thresholds alone.

### [SplatQ](14415-splatq.md)
[SplatQ](#14415-splatq.md) is a post-training pruning framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses spatial quality imbalance and ignores joint deletion effects inherent in global Top-K selection methods. It partitions Gaussians into size-limited blocks based on spatial and appearance similarity, allocates retention quotas to balance regional budgets, and uses a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to jointly select Gaussians within each block, thereby accounting for pairwise interactions and overlapping contributions.

### [Attribute Pruning](18516-attribute-pruning.md)
[Attribute pruning](#18516-attribute-pruning.md) selectively reduces the storage and computational overhead of per-Gaussian attributes, primarily [spherical harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) (SH) coefficients, to optimize memory usage and rendering efficiency. Unlike [Pruning and Reduction](14909-pruning-and-reduction.md) which focuses on removing entire primitives, attribute pruning retains the Gaussian primitives but simplifies their representation. It differs from [SplatQ](14415-splatq.md) by focusing on the dimensionality of the attribute vectors rather than [quantization](#5935-quantization.md) of the entire data structure, and from [Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting](13983-vertex-level-pruning-in-mixed-primitive-gaussian-splatting.md) by operating on the standard [Gaussian representation](#5918-gaussian-based-representation.md) without changing the primitive type.

### Vertex Pruning
#### definition
- [S1, unofficial] A pruning mechanism designed to support mixed-primitive-based learning, as standard pruning is incompatible with mixed primitives.
#### step
- [S1, unofficial] Prune vertices of the mixed primitives to optimize the representation.

### Gaussian Reduction with Learnable Mask
#### definition
- [S2] A method to reduce the number of Gaussians using a learnable mask during optimization, targeting small-sized kernels for removal.
#### step
- [S2] Apply binary masks M to the opacities and scale attributes of the kernels at every densification step.
- [S2] Use [residual vector quantization](#12711-residual-vector-quantization-r-vq.md) with L stages of [vector quantization](#907-vector-quantization.md) for geometric attributes like scale and rotation.
- [S2] Represent view-dependent colors via a grid-based neural field using [hash grids](#936-hash-grids.md) for input positions, features, and view direction, fed into an MLP.
#### formula
- [S2] The [end-to-end loss](#10621-overall-training-loss.md) is: $L = L_{ren} + \lambda_m L_m + L_r + L_s$, where $L_{ren}$ is [L1+SSIM loss](#2890-l1-ssim-loss.md), $L_m$ is masking loss ($\frac{1}{N} \sum \sigma(m_n)$), and $L_r, L_s$ are rotation and scale objective functions.
#### parameter
- [S2] $\epsilon$: Masking threshold for the sigmoid function in the learnable mask.
- [S2] $\lambda_m$: Weight for the masking loss term, typically $5 \times 10^{-4}$.

### 3DGS Visibility Pruning
#### definition
- [S2] Application of [visibility-based pruning](#4521-visibility-based-pruning.md) to 3D Gaussian Splatting, using Gaussian centroids as reference points for visibility calculation.
#### step
- [S2] Represent each Gaussian kernel by its centroid position, [scaling matrix](#4126-scaling-matrix-construction.md) $S$, and rotation matrix $R$ defining the covariance $\Sigma$.
- [S2] Use the Gaussian centroids as the 3D points $p_i$ in the [visibility mask computation](#9086-visible-zone-algorithm.md) algorithm.

### Visibility List-Based Rendering
#### definition
- [S3] A post-processing step that filters out Gaussians not visible to the current camera view to increase rendering speed without affecting image quality.
#### step
- [S3] Perform visibility filtering as a post-processing step on the Gaussian representation before rendering.
#### number
- [S3] On MipNeRF360 scenes, achieves up to 10% mean [FPS](#7182-farthest-point-sampling-fps.md) speedup (e.g., 410 FPS vs 373 FPS without filtering).
- [S3] On Zip-NeRF scenes, achieves up to 45% improvement in rendering speed (e.g., 630 FPS vs 435 FPS without filtering).
#### comparison
- [S3] Provides significant speedup on large-scale scenes (Zip-NeRF) compared to central object-focused scenes (MipNeRF360), making it particularly important for large scenes.

## Background
Pruning and reduction techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as the method scaled to large, complex scenes where the number of Gaussians could reach millions, leading to high memory consumption and rendering latency. Early 3DGS implementations relied on opacity-based culling during the forward pass, but this did not reduce the storage size of the model. Subsequent research introduced methods to actively prune Gaussians during training or post-training to create more compact representations.

Vertex-level pruning was introduced in the context of Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting to handle topological redundancy in non-standard primitive types (triangles and lines) [S1, unofficial]. Standard opacity pruning is insufficient for these primitives because their geometric structure (vertices) carries more information than a single scalar opacity.

Visibility-based pruning and reduction with learnable masks were proposed to address the inefficiency of retaining Gaussians that do not contribute to the final image from any camera view or have negligible impact on rendering quality [S2]. These methods integrate pruning into the optimization loop, using masks to suppress small or occluded kernels.

Visibility list-based rendering was introduced as a post-processing optimization to accelerate rendering by pre-filtering the Gaussian list based on camera frustum and occlusion, achieving significant FPS improvements without altering the scene representation [S3].
